1.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **The burden of the wilderness of the sea** to introduce a new oracle. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [A message about]

The point of this comparison is that just as **whirlwinds in the Negev** are swift and destructive, so is the invading army that comes from the wilderness. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As swiftly and destructively as whirlwinds sweep through the Negev]

The pronoun **it** refers to the invading army of Elam and Media, which Isaiah speaks of more explicitly in the next verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [an invading army comes]

2.note: The expression **has been declared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has declared]

Isaiah is using a construction in which a subject and its verb come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this.

3.note: Isaiah is speaking as if his **loins** were literally full of **writhing**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am filled with intense anguish]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the pangs of one birthing** are intense and overwhelming, so is the anguish that has seized Isaiah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like the intense and overwhelming pangs of a woman giving birth]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [What I hear bends me over; indeed, what I see causes deep dismay]

4.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My thoughts wander]

Isaiah is using this possessive form to describe **twilight** as the object of his **desire**, that is, as something he has desired. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The twilight I have desired]

Isaiah is speaking as if he had actually desired for it to be **twilight** or evening. He is using that time of day, when people in this culture stopped working, to mean a time of rest or relief. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The time of rest that I have desired] or [The relief that I have desired]
The pronoun **he** refers by anticipation to “the Lord” in verse 6. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The Lord has made trembling for me]

5.q: עָרֹ֧ךְ הַ⁠שֻּׁלְחָ֛ן צָפֹ֥ה הַ⁠צָּפִ֖ית אָכ֣וֹל שָׁתֹ֑ה
5.note: This is a direct quotation from an unidentified speaker. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing such a direct quotation in your language.

5.q: עָרֹ֧ךְ הַ⁠שֻּׁלְחָ֛ן צָפֹ֥ה הַ⁠צָּפִ֖ית אָכ֣וֹל שָׁתֹ֑ה
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. The UST models one way to do that.
This is another direct quotation from an unidentified speaker. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing such a direct quotation in your language.

6.note: The phrase **thus the Lord said to me** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

7.note: The Lord is repeating forms of the verb **attend** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [he shall pay close attention, very close attention]

8.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “And the lion called out.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “the one seeing called out.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The watchman is repeating the pronoun **I** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that he himself is faithfully standing watch. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I myself am standing]

The watchman is repeating the pronoun **I** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that he himself is faithfully stationed at his post. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I myself am stationed]

8.q: עַל־מִצְפֶּ֣ה אֲדֹנָ֗⁠י אָנֹכִ֞י עֹמֵ֤ד תָּמִיד֙ יוֹמָ֔ם וְ⁠עַל־מִ֨שְׁמַרְתִּ֔⁠י אָנֹכִ֥י נִצָּ֖ב כָּל־הַ⁠לֵּילֽוֹת
8.note: The watchman says **I am standing continually by day** and **I am stationed all of the night** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [I am faithfully standing watch during the day, and I am faithfully stationed at my guardpost during the night]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** is loud and commanding, so is the watchman’s cry. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And he called out with a loud and commanding voice, like a lion]

9.note: The watchman is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [And look]

The phrase **And he answered and said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

The speaker is repeating the verb **fallen** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Babylon has certainly fallen!]

**Babylon** here represents the Babylonian empire and its government. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The Babylonian empire has fallen, has fallen]
The word **one** does not refer to a specific person. It refers generally to the conquering forces. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [they have shattered]

10.note: Isaiah is speaking as if his people were grain on a **threshing floor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My people who have been crushed like grain]

Isaiah is using **son of** as a common expression of the culture to indicate that a person has a certain characteristic. In this case, Isaiah’s people have the characteristic of belonging to his **threshing floor**, meaning they are his own people who have endured severe oppression similar to what happens to grain that is being threshed. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the people of my threshing floor] or [and my severely oppressed people]

Isaiah is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control Yahweh. Rather Moses is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God whom Israel worships]

11.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **The burden of Dumah** to introduce a new oracle. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [A message about]

For poetic effect, Isaiah is rearranging the consonants in the name Edom to make the name **Dumah**, which means “silence.” There was a different place, a desert oasis, whose name actually was Dumah, but Isaiah means the nation of Edom, not that oasis. The UST models one way to clarify this.
The word **One** refers to an unidentified person calling from the region of Seir. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Someone calling to me]

The caller is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [How far along is the night] or [What is left of the night]

The caller is using the question form to express his desperate plea to know how much longer the suffering will last. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Watchman, the night is so long!]

11.q: שֹׁמֵר֙ מַה מִ⁠לַּ֔יְלָה שֹׁמֵ֖ר מַה מִ⁠לֵּֽיל
11.note: The caller is repeating the question **Watchman, what of the night?** in order to intensify his expression of urgency. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Watchman, I beg you, how much longer will the night last?]

12.q: אָמַ֣ר שֹׁמֵ֔ר אָתָ֥ה בֹ֖קֶר וְ⁠גַם לָ֑יְלָה אִם תִּבְעָי֥וּ⁠ן בְּעָ֖יוּ שֻׁ֥בוּ אֵתָֽיוּ
12.note: The **watchman** uses the phrase **and also** here to indicate a contrast between **morning** (a time of brief relief) and **night** (renewed suffering). In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The watchman said, “Morning comes, but so does night. If you would inquire, inquire; return, come]

The watchman is speaking as if a brief time of relief were **morning** and as if renewed suffering were **night**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A time of relief will come, and also a time of suffering]

The watchman is presenting a possible condition, that the people of Edom may inquire further about their situation. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [If you want to inquire, then inquire; come back and ask]

13.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **The burden against Arabia** to introduce a new oracle. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [A message about Arabia]

14.q: לִ⁠קְרַ֥את צָמֵ֖א הֵתָ֣יוּ מָ֑יִם יֹשְׁבֵי֙ אֶ֣רֶץ תֵּימָ֔א
14.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who is being addressed (**dwellers of the land of Tema**) before the command to **bring water**. Alternate translation: [Dwellers of the land of Tema, bring water to meet the thirsty one]

The pronoun **its** refers to Tema, while the pronoun **they** refers to the dwellers of the land of Tema. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [With Tema’s bread, the dwellers of Tema met the fugitive]

15.q: כִּֽי מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י חֲרָב֖וֹת נָדָ֑דוּ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י חֶ֣רֶב נְטוּשָׁ֗ה וּ⁠מִ⁠פְּנֵי֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת דְּרוּכָ֔ה וּ⁠מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י כֹּ֥בֶד מִלְחָמָֽה
15.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because they have fled from the face of swords, from the face of a drawn sword and from the face of a tread bow and from the face of the heaviness of war]

15.q: כִּֽי־מִ⁠פְּנֵ֥י חֲרָב֖וֹת נָדָ֑דוּ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י ׀ חֶ֣רֶב נְטוּשָׁ֗ה וּ⁠מִ⁠פְּנֵי֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת דְּרוּכָ֔ה וּ⁠מִ⁠פְּנֵ֖י כֹּ֥בֶד מִלְחָמָֽה
15.note: Isaiah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For because of swords they have fled, because of a drawn sword and because of a tread bow and because of the heaviness of war]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **heaviness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how heavy war is]

16.note: Here, **the glory of Kedar** represents “the military power and greatness of Kedar.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all of the military power and greatness of Kedar]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the years of a hired one** are precisely counted and carefully tracked, so the time until the fall of Kedar will be precisely measured. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Within one year, as precisely counted as the years of a hired worker]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the glorious things of]

17.note: The Lord is using a chain of possessive forms to describe the **remnant** of the **number of the archer**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the surviving archers]

The Lord is speaking as if the descendants of Kedar were literally his **sons**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Kedar]
The phrase **has spoken** concludes Yahweh’s direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the conclusion of direct quotations in your language.
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:10. Alternate translation: [the God whom Israel worships]
